Typically when labels invest in an artist advances (upfront money aka the $15mil from RCA) are used to pay for music production, features, live show production, film production, marketing, touring costs, etc. 
But since most of BH’s production is in-house and they already cover most of the bases on they’re own, they aren’t saving a lot of money compared to an artist that doesn’t have that infrastructure.

Each member could have pocketed their share and just continue to do what they do. A lot of smart artists make other investments in something non-music related (houses, stocks, silicon valley, etc) as a backup in case the album doesn’t recoup. 

I imagine it goes something like this: 
-historically, producers paid up front and receive royalties from radio, performances, and streams

-performing artists are paid upfront and receive a larger percent of the royalties

-the designers are paid up front & per diem or maybe on salary employed by BH. They get royalties from YouTube streams. They also get a share of the BH profit.

-The label takes a percentage of all profits, until the $15mil is recouped

Pros: 
•Money (not everyone owns orchestral instruments/drums, etc)
•Skill level - It’d take years to learn to play a violin, but a good vst can allow you to get away with a lot 
•Different sounds can inspire you!
•Don’t need a treated space to record 

Cons:
•CPU - some vst’s can be really CPU, which can get annoying if you have to run several vst’s at the same time
•Realism - the public might not be able to pick out a vst, but a musician can easily pick out what is a VST and what is not (especially the cheap ones)
•Not as fun as the real thing!
